details: Levelized Cost of Electricity (LCOE): all-in cost per unit of electricity over plant lifetime; nuclear LCOE (new build; 2024 estimate): $70-120/MWh (high range: US; Western Europe); $50-80/MWh (South Korea; China where construction costs lower); comparison: solar PV utility-scale: $30-60/MWh; onshore wind: $25-50/MWh; offshore wind: $80-150/MWh; combined cycle gas (CCGT): $50-80/MWh; NUCLEAR COST COMPONENTS: (1) Capital (overnight construction): 50-70% of LCOE; typical: $5,000-10,000/kW; (2) O&M (operation and maintenance): 15-25%; (3) Fuel: 10-15%; (4) Decommissioning: 5%; (5) Interest during construction: significant for long-build projects; RBMK original cost (Soviet): highly subsidized; state-owned; costs not transparent; estimated equivalent: $1,500-3,000/kW in today's dollars; Soviet RBMK economics: designed to be cheap (no containment = saved $500-800/kW in capital)
chernobyl_application: Nuclear economics context: nuclear LCOE varies enormously by: (1) Construction time (longer = more interest); (2) Interest rate (higher = more expensive); (3) Construction experience (learning curve: nth-of-kind vs first-of-kind); (4) Safety standards (post-Fukushima upgrades added $1-2B per plant); (5) Regulation (10yr licensing → interest costs); LCOE excludes: system integration costs (backup for variable renewables); grid infrastructure; US comparison: existing nuclear $20-35/MWh (no capital cost); new nuclear $80-120/MWh; solar $30-50/MWh; conclusion: existing nuclear = cheapest source; new nuclear = expensive vs solar/wind; policy implication: lifetime extension (LTO) of existing nuclear = most economical nuclear pathway; new build economic only with: (1) Carbon price; (2) Firm power premium; (3) State financing (as in France; China; Korea)
source: nuclear_power_global_context_REAL.csv; chernobyl_economic_impact_REAL.csv; IEA Projected Costs of Generating Electricity 2022

details: Nuclear plant decommissioning costs: international comparison: PWR/BWR decommissioning: $300-800M per unit (US NRC estimates; 2024); immediate decommissioning: more expensive upfront but less total (labor; project costs); deferred decommissioning (SAFSTOR): wait 30-60yr for decay → lower radiation → lower cost; total decommissioning cost: UK (BNFL/NDA): £100B for all UK nuclear legacy; US NRC: utilities required to fund decommissioning trust funds during operation; Chernobyl decommissioning total estimate: $2-4B (SSE CHNPP estimate) for Units 1-4 + 5+6; but: unique challenges: corium cannot be removed; graphite stack radioactive; highly contaminated building structures; actual cost likely $5-10B over full decommissioning period (2026-2064); EBRD + bilateral funding: committed €2.3B through 2026; additional funding needed: ~€1-2B for 2026-2064 period
chernobyl_application: Chernobyl decommissioning as global nuclear industry test case: (1) First time a severely damaged reactor (Unit 4) will be decommissioned; technical template being developed; (2) Units 1-3: standard decommissioning but in highly contaminated environment; (3) Fuel removed: ISF-2 loading (target: complete 2028); (4) After ISF-2 complete: begin Unit 1-3 active decommissioning (remote tools; robotic systems); (5) NSC: first-ever movable nuclear structure; design life 100yr; (6) Corium: no removal plan; in-situ monitoring + NSC = sufficient for this generation; (7) Target end state 2064: 'brown field' (unrestricted access but NSC over Unit 4 remains); entire process = global nuclear decommissioning training ground; Ringhals 1+2 (Sweden); Dresden 1+2 (US) = more standard examples; Chernobyl = most complex nuclear decommissioning in world history

details: Nuclear vs renewable energy economics: critical distinction: LCOE vs LCOS (Levelized Cost of Storage) + system value: nuclear: 24/7 firm capacity; capacity factor 85-92%; dispatchable; maintains grid stability; renewable: variable (solar: 20-30% CF; wind: 25-45% CF); requires backup (gas; storage; demand response; interconnection); system integration cost: adding >30% wind/solar to grid requires backup capacity → increases system cost; this 'integration cost' not captured in LCOE; estimates: integration cost adds $10-30/MWh to renewable LCOE at high penetrations; nuclear system value premium: ~$20-40/MWh above LCOE for firm capacity in high-renewable grids; nuclear + renewable complementarity: France (70% nuclear) + Germany (45% renewable) + interconnection = more stable European grid than either alone; IEA Net Zero: requires nuclear doubling by 2050 as 'firm clean power'
chernobyl_application: Post-Chernobyl economic effect on nuclear: 1986-2010: new nuclear construction effectively ceased in Western countries; US: no new construction order completed 1979-2012 (>30yr); Europe: similar pause; economic reason: cost overruns (Three Mile Island cleanup; Chernobyl awareness) + public opposition + regulatory uncertainty → investment community avoided nuclear; opportunity cost: had nuclear continued at 1970s pace → would have ~50% nuclear globally by 2000 → ~3-5 billion tonnes less CO₂ per year; ESTIMATED CO₂ IMPACT of nuclear pause post-Chernobyl (counterfactual): Hansen et al. 2013 (Environ Sci Technol): estimate 1.8M premature deaths from air pollution AVOIDED by nuclear 1971-2009; counterfactual: if nuclear replaced by coal → 7.4M additional deaths; nuclear moratorium after Chernobyl = substitution to coal globally → health impact > Chernobyl itself
source: nuclear_power_global_context_REAL.csv; chernobyl_economic_impact_REAL.csv; IEA 2023 World Energy Outlook; Hansen 2013

details: ISF-2 (Interim Spent Fuel Storage Facility) economics: construction cost: €168M (Holtec International contract); funded by: EBRD Shelter Fund (primary) + bilateral donors (US: $45M); construction period: 2003-2020 (17yr; major delays); operational: 2020+; loading rate: ~1700 assemblies per year; target completion: 2028 (21,217 assemblies); capital cost per assembly: €168M / 21,217 = €7,920/assembly; operating cost: minimal (passive cooling; security; monitoring): ~€5M/yr; total lifecycle cost (2020-2060): ~€168M + €5M/yr × 40yr = €368M; compared to: wet pool ISF-1 (continuing operation cost): €10-15M/yr maintenance + active cooling; ISF-2 advantage: passive → zero cooling electricity required after sealing; lifecycle cost per assembly at 100yr: €368M / 21,217 ÷ (30,000 kWh/assembly output) = negligible per kWh generated; spent fuel as financial liability: $1M per assembly estimated final disposal cost in DGR
chernobyl_application: ISF-2 vs ISF-1 cost comparison: ISF-1 (wet pool): built 1986; operating 40yr; cooling electricity: ~50 kWh/m³/yr × 3,000 m³ pools × 3 units = ~4.5 GWh/yr; cost at $50/MWh = $225,000/yr electricity alone; ISF-1 water treatment: $2M/yr; structural maintenance: $5M/yr; total: ~$8M/yr; ISF-2 passive: monitoring + security: $3M/yr (estimate); ISF-2 lower long-term cost; ISF-2 safety advantage: passive (no pumps = no failure mode requiring backup power); Fukushima Unit 4 spent fuel pool: active cooling failed after tsunami → pool temperature rising → potential hydrogen generation; near-miss; ISF-2 design: eliminates this scenario entirely; 4,668 kg Pu-239 in ISF-2 at completion: reactor-grade; safeguards monitored; zero weapons utility; financial value of Pu-239 if weapons-grade: ~$6,000/g → $28B total; actual value = zero (cannot be extracted or used)
